content: Erythema multiforme is a dermatological condition that arises due to an allergic reaction or an infection. Symptoms of Erythema Multiforme: Patients may experience fever. A general feeling of being unwell is common. Skin itching is frequently reported. Joint pain may occur. Multiple skin lesions are characteristic and may: Appear suddenly and have a tendency to recur. Spread across the body. Present as nodules, papules, or macules, sometimes resembling hives. Exhibit a central sore surrounded by pale red rings, often described as a target, iris, or bulls-eye lesion. Contain vesicles or blisters of varying sizes (bullae). Be located on the upper body, legs, arms, palms, hands, or feet. Involve the face or lips. Typically appear symmetrically on both sides of the body. Other associated symptoms may include: Bloodshot eyes. Dryness of the eyes. Burning, itching, or discharge from the eyes. Eye pain. Mouth sores. Vision disturbances. Causes of Erythema Multiforme: Erythema multiforme is a hypersensitivity reaction triggered by medications, infections, or illnesses. Medications that may cause this condition include: Barbiturates. Penicillins. Phenytoin. Sulfonamides. Infections associated with erythema multiforme include: Herpes simplex virus. Mycoplasma infections. The exact pathophysiology remains unclear, but it is believed to involve damage to the skin's blood vessels, followed by injury to the surrounding skin tissues. There are two forms of erythema multiforme: Erythema multiforme minor: A less severe form, often associated with herpes simplex or mycoplasma infections. Erythema multiforme major: A more severe form, also known as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which is typically caused by adverse drug reactions rather than infections. Risk Factors: Erythema multiforme primarily affects children and young adults. Diagnosis: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on the appearance of the skin lesions, particularly when there is a history of risk factors or related conditions. Diagnostic tests may include: Nikolsky's sign. Skin lesion biopsy with microscopic examination of the tissue. When to Seek Emergency Care: Immediate medical attention is required if symptoms of erythema multiforme are present. If a large area of the body is affected, it constitutes a medical emergency. Treatment Options: The goals of treatment are to: Manage the underlying illness causing the condition. Prevent secondary infections. Alleviate symptoms. For mild cases, treatment may include: Antihistamines to control itching. Moist compresses applied to the skin. Oral antiviral medications if herpes simplex is the cause. Over-the-counter medications like acetaminophen to reduce fever and discomfort. Topical anesthetics, especially for mouth lesions, to ease pain and facilitate eating and drinking. For severe cases, treatment may involve: Antibiotics to manage skin infections. Corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. Hospitalization, often in an intensive care or burn care unit, for conditions like Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. Intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) to halt disease progression. Good hygiene practices and avoiding contact with others can help prevent secondary infections. In cases where large areas of the body are affected, skin grafting may be beneficial. Prognosis: Mild forms of erythema multiforme typically resolve within 2 to 6 weeks but may recur. Severe forms, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, are more challenging to treat and carry a high mortality rate.
